segments.translit: jñānānandapramodabharastimitahṛdayaḥ siddhācāryo hi śāntis tam evārthaṃ janārthāya pratipādayati —
segments.translation: The [siddha]{siddha} master [Śāntipāda]{p-santi}, his heart soaked with the fullness of delight in the [joy]{ananda} of [knowledge]{jnana}, sets forth that very point for the sake of people:
segments.note: Munidatta (cp.26.m1) introduces the song as the teaching of the [siddha]{siddha} master [Śāntipāda]{p-santi} (a siddha is an accomplished tantric adept), whose heart is soaked with delight in the [joy]{ananda} of [knowledge]{jnana}, and who sets forth that same point for the sake of people.

flags.note: The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has ye shes kyi dga' ba'i bde bas gang zhing brlan pa, ‘filled and moistened with the bliss of the joy of knowledge’. It supports taking stimita as ‘soaked, moistened’ rather than ‘motionless’, has no word for ‘heart’ (hṛdaya), and gives bde ba, ‘bliss’, for one of the two joy-words (ānanda, pramoda).
tam evārtham, ‘that very point’: Munidatta does not say which point (cp.26.m1), whether the song's own or that of the songs before it. I translate literally.

segments.translit:
tuletyādi | prakṛtidoṣatvāt tulanayogyatrailokyaṃ kāyavākcittaṃ | asya kampākampādibhedenāvayavinam ekapramāṇopapannaṃ kṛtvā mayāvayavasya ṣaḍaṃśasādhanaḥ kṛtaḥ | sa evāvayavaparamāṇupuñjasya paramāṇoḥ ṣaḍaṅgatābhāvena taṃ dhūtvā dhūtvā niravaram iti niravayavaṃ sūcitaṃ | tathā cāhetukatvāt tasya cittasya hetvantaraṃ na prāpyate | śāntipādo vadati bhāvopalambhābhāvena kiṃ bhāvyate |
tathā ca prajñāparicchede vicārita ityādi |
segments.translation: “[Cotton]{tula}…” and the rest. Because of the [faults of nature]{prakrtidosa}, the [three worlds]{trailokya}, [body, speech and mind]{kaya-vak-citta}, are fit to be weighed. Having made their [whole]{avayavin}, through the distinction of moving and unmoving and so on, a matter settled by a single [valid cognition]{pramana}, I have proved that the [part]{avayava} has six parts. The same proof holds for the [atom]{paramanu} of the heap of atoms that makes up the part: since the atom has six parts, after [carding]{dhuni} it and carding it, the word niravara indicates that it is [partless]{niravayava}. And so, since it is without [cause]{hetu}, no further cause of that [mind]{citta} is found. [Śāntipāda]{p-santi} says: when there is no [apprehension]{upalambha} of things, what is to be meditated on? So too in the [Chapter on Wisdom]{tx-prajnapariccheda}: “When examined…” and so on.
segments.note: Munidatta (cp.26.m2) sets beside the cotton [body, speech and mind]{kaya-vak-citta}, the three worlds, ‘fit to be weighed’ (a play on tulā). He divides the whole, shows that part and atom have six parts, and cards the atom again and again until the [partless]{niravayava} is indicated. That mind has no further cause; with nothing apprehended, nothing remains to meditate on.

citations.quoted: vicārita ityādi: “When examined…” and so on
citations.work: A ‘Chapter on Wisdom’ (prajñāpariccheda), so named by Munidatta (cp.26.m2); the work is not identified. A guess to be checked: the ninth chapter of Śāntideva's Bodhicaryāvatāra, whose title is the chapter on the perfection of wisdom. Only the opening word is quoted, and I have supplied nothing more.

flags.note: Bearing on line 2a (herua): Munidatta's sentence tathā cāhetukatvāt tasya cittasya hetvantaraṃ na prāpyate (cp.26.m2) follows the refrain word for word: tathā ca for tauṣe, hetvantara, ‘a further cause’, for herua, and na prāpyate for ṇa pābiai. He says nothing of Heruka. This implies he read herua as, or glossed it by, a word for ‘cause’ (hetu); it gives no support to the draft's ‘Heruka’. The Tibetan line has gzugs, ‘form’, for herua. The Tibetan comment keeps rgyu, ‘cause’, but renders hetvantaraṃ na prāpyate as rjes la thob pa med, ‘there is no subsequent attainment’. I have not touched the song draft.

Munidatta's tulanayogya, ‘fit to be weighed’ (cp.26.m2), plays on the cited word tulā, ‘cotton’ (compare tulā, ‘balance’); English loses the play. He sets the three worlds, body, speech and mind, beside the cited word without an explicit ‘X means Y’, so I have not listed it as an equation. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has tshad mas gzhal bar rig pa, ‘fit to be measured by valid cognition’, in line with its tshad ma for tulā in line 1a, and joins the two with ‘and’ ('jig rten gsum dang lus ngag yid, ‘the three worlds and body, speech and mind’) where the Sanskrit sets them in apposition.

asya kampākampādibhedenāvayavinam ekapramāṇopapannaṃ kṛtvā is compressed. I take it as ‘having made their whole, through the distinction of moving and unmoving, a matter settled by one valid cognition’: the Buddhist argument that a whole whose parts at once move and do not move cannot be one. Another possible reading is ‘treating the whole as established by a single valid cognition’, the opponent's view, which is then refuted. The Tibetan has cha shas can gcig tshad mas skyes par byas pa, ‘the one whole made to arise by valid cognition’. It has no first person for mayā, ‘by me’, and has rang bzhin, ‘nature’, at that point. The first person, Munidatta speaking in the poet's voice (cp.26.m2; compare praveśitaṃ mayā, cp.26.m3), is found only in the Sanskrit.

ṣaḍaṅgatābhāvena divides two ways. I follow ṣaḍaṅgatā-bhāvena, ‘because (the atom) has six parts’, since ‘the same proof’ of six parts is being applied to the atom. The alternative is ṣaḍaṅgatā-abhāvena, ‘through (its) nonexistence, being six-parted’. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has rdul phran cha drug tu dngos po med par phye zhing phye bas, ‘dividing the atom again and again into six parts, as without entity’, which supports abhāva. The edition spells ṣaṛ- for ṣaḍ- and restores paramāṇo[ḥ]; I accept the restoration.

dhūtvā dhūtvā is literally ‘having shaken, having shaken’ (Sanskrit dhū). It repeats the song's dhuṇi dhuṇi, so I render it ‘carding’ (cp.26.m2). The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has phye zhing phye ba, ‘dividing again and again’.

Bearing on line 2b: Munidatta's bhāvopalambhābhāvena kiṃ bhāvyate, ‘when there is no apprehension of things, what is to be meditated on?’ (cp.26.m2), agrees with the draft. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) splits the compound: dngos po de la dmigs pa dang dngos po med pa la ci zhig bsgom par bya, ‘in apprehending that thing, and in nonbeing, what is to be meditated on?’

vicārita ityādi: before ityādi, the form may stand for vicāritaḥ, ‘examined’, or vicārite, ‘when (it) is examined’. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has rnam par dpyad byas na, ‘when (or if) it is examined’. I translate ‘When examined…’ and supply nothing of the rest of the passage.

segments.translit:
dvitīyapadena tam evārthaṃ dṛḍhayati — tuladhuṇītyādi | tadvicārapramāṇato 'py avayavādikaṃ dattvā | śūnyeti | prabhāsvare cittaṃ praveśitaṃ mayā | taṃ prabhāsvaraṃ gṛhītvā caṭāriva iti | ātmagrahabhāvyabhāvakarūpaṃ bādhitam iti |
tathā dvikalpe —
nāsti bhāvako na bhāvyo 'stītyādi |
segments.translation: With the second [verse]{pada} he makes that same point firm: “[Carding]{dhuni} the [cotton]{tula}…” and the rest. Through the [valid cognition]{pramana} of that [examination]{vicara}, too, the [parts]{avayava} and the rest are given up. “Into [emptiness]{sunyata}”: I made the [mind]{citta} enter [clear light]{prabhasvara}. Having taken up that clear light, “I put a stop to”: that is, the form of [grasping at a self]{atmagraha}, as [object of meditation and meditator]{bhavya-bhavaka}, is refuted. So too in the [Hevajra]{tx-hevajra}: “There is no meditator, nor is there anything to meditate on…” and so on.
segments.note: Munidatta (cp.26.m3) takes the second carding as giving up the parts through examination by [valid cognition]{pramana}. ‘Into emptiness’ means ‘I made the mind enter [clear light]{prabhasvara}’. Having taken up that clear light, ‘I put a stop to’ means that self-grasping, as object of meditation and meditator, is refuted. The [Hevajra]{tx-hevajra} agrees: there is no meditator, nothing to meditate on.

equations.en: clear light, into which the mind is made to enter
refuted (bādhita): the form of grasping at a self, as object of meditation and meditator

citations.quoted: nāsti bhāvako na bhāvyo 'stītyādi: “There is no meditator, nor is there anything to meditate on…” and so on
citations.work: Hevajra Tantra, which Munidatta calls the Dvikalpa (cp.26.m3); quoted by its opening words only, and I have supplied nothing more

flags.note: Bearing on line 3b (caṭāriu): Munidatta cites caṭāriva and glosses it with bādhitam, ‘refuted, struck down’, whose object is ‘the form of grasping at a self, as object of meditation and meditator’ (cp.26.m3). So he took caṭāriu as a verb of destroying or annulling, and apaṇā, ‘own’, as the self of self-grasping. What is taken up again (puna laiām̐) is for him the clear light (taṃ prabhāsvaraṃ gṛhītvā), not the cotton. The Tibetan line ('gog par byed) and comment ('gog pa) have ‘stop’. The draft's ‘put a stop to’ fits his verb, but his object is self-grasping, not the self.

dattvā, ‘having given’, is odd as a paraphrase of the carding (cp.26.m3). I take it as ‘giving up’: the parts and the rest are relinquished through examination. It may be a slip for dhūtvā, ‘having shaken (carded)’, as in cp.26.m2; ধূত্বা and দত্ত্বা look alike. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has 'byin pa, ‘drawing out, extracting’, and cites the lemma as tshad mas brtags, ‘examined by valid cognition’, its own rendering of tulā dhuṇi.

Munidatta's praveśitaṃ mayā, ‘I made (the mind) enter’ (cp.26.m3), confirms the first person of ahāriu in line 3a and makes the mind its object. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has 'od gsal la sems rab tu zhugs pa, ‘the mind entered clear light’, without ‘by me’. It attaches bdag gis, ‘by me’, to the next clause instead: de la bdag gis 'od gsal bzung nas, ‘there, I took up clear light’.

The Tibetan of the Hevajra quotation, bsgom med sgom pa po yang med, puts the object of meditation first: ‘no object of meditation, and no meditator either’. The sense is the same. The edition spells dṛṛhayati for dṛḍhayati.

segments.translit:
tṛtīyapadena mārgasyānuśaṃsām āha —
bahaletyādi | advayatvād asmin mārgavare dvayākāraṃ na vidyate | ata eva śāntipādo hi vadati | bālo hy ajño 'smin dharme na (ṇa) praviśati sudūra eva | athavā bālavat rekhāsandhimātram atra na vidyate |
tathā ca nāgārjunapādāḥ —
sauśīryyante kāye ityādi |
segments.translation: With the third [verse]{pada} he speaks in [praise]{anusamsa} of the [path]{marga}: “On the broad…” and the rest. Because it is [nondual]{advaya}, on this excellent path the [dual aspect]{dvayakara} does not exist. That is why [Śāntipāda]{p-santi} says: the fool, the ignorant one, does not enter this [dharma]{dharma}; he stays far away. Or else: not even a seam like a hair, the mere join of a line, exists here. As the revered [Nāgārjuna]{p-nagarjuna} says: “…hollowness … in the [body]{body}…” and so on.
segments.note: Munidatta (cp.26.m4) reads the couplet as praise of the path: being [nondual]{advaya}, this excellent path has no dual aspect. He reads the hair's tip two ways: the fool, the ignorant one, does not enter this [dharma]{dharma} and stays far off; or not even a seam like a hair exists here. He then cites [Nāgārjuna]{p-nagarjuna} on the body.

equations.en: the fool, the ignorant one (ajña), who does not enter this dharma and stays far from it

equations.src: bāla (athavā bālavat, ‘or else, like a hair’)
equations.en: like a hair: not even a seam, the mere join of a line, exists here

citations.quoted: sauśīryyante kāye ityādi: “…hollowness … in the body…” and so on
citations.work: A verse that Munidatta attributes to Nāgārjuna (cp.26.m4); he does not name the work and I have not identified it. Only the opening words are quoted, and their first word is doubtful.

flags.note: Bearing on line 4a (dui māra): Munidatta's paraphrase advayatvād asmin mārgavare dvayākāraṃ na vidyate (cp.26.m4), ‘because it is nondual, on this excellent path the dual aspect does not exist’, puts dvayākāra, ‘appearance as two’, where the song has dui māra. He also puts mārgavara, ‘excellent path’, for bāṭa, and na vidyate, ‘does not exist’, for na diśaa. He never mentions Māra. This implies he read or understood the words as ‘two (aspects)’, not ‘two Māras’. The Tibetan agrees: its line has rnam pa gnyis, ‘two aspects’, and its comment rnam pa gnyis su med pa. Neither supports the draft's ‘two Māras’.

Bearing on line 4a (bahala): Munidatta cites the word without glossing it (cp.26.m4). The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) cites the lemma as 'bab, ‘flowing, descending’, and its line has 'bab lam, ‘the flowing (or descending) road’. It read the word as coming from vah-, ‘flow, carry’, not as ‘broad’. Bengali script does not distinguish b from v, so the commentary's বহলে can also be read vahale.

The two readings of line 4b. Munidatta first takes bāla as ‘fool’, glossed ajña, ‘ignorant’: the fool does not enter this dharma and stays far off. Then, ‘or else’, he takes it as ‘like a hair’: not even a seam, the mere join of a line, is here (cp.26.m4). The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) keeps only the hair. For the first reading it has 'dir skra'i rtse mo'i cha'i chos kyis zhugs na de'ang ring ba nyid do, roughly ‘if one enters this dharma by so much as a hair-tip's portion, even that is far off’, with no ‘fool’ and no negative. For the second it has skra'i rtse kha'i mtshams kyi cha 'dir med pa, ‘here there is no portion of a hair-tip's join’, with no clear word for ‘line’ (rekhā).

The first word of the Nāgārjuna citation sauśīryyante kāye ityādi is doubtful. I take it as sauṣiryaṃ, ‘hollowness, porousness’ (from suṣira, ‘hollow’), followed by te, ‘your’, or ante, ‘within’, and translate only ‘hollowness … in the body’. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has de yi lus la khong seng med, ‘in his body there is no hollow’. Its negative and its ‘his’ are absent from the quoted Sanskrit words; the negative may have stood in the unquoted rest. I have not supplied the rest of the verse. Munidatta introduces it with tathā ca, ‘and so’, directly after the reading ‘not even a seam’ (cp.26.m4).

bālo hy ajño: hi may mark a gloss (‘a fool, that is, one who is ignorant’) or be emphatic (‘for the fool, the ignorant one…’); the sense is the same. Shastri prints na (ṇa), giving both spellings of the negative; I translate through it.
The edition prints mārgāsya; I read mārgasya, ‘of the path’.

segments.translit:
caturthapadena svarūpopalambham āha —
kājetyādi | siddhācāryo hi śāntiḥ svayaṃ kāryakāraṇarahitatvāt | anuttarapadaṃ vadati | eṣā hi yuktiḥ | pramāṇopapannā sadguruprasādād anuttarapadaṃ svayaṃ jñāyate |
tathā ca dvikalpe —
ātmanā jñāyate puṇyāt guruparvopasevayā || 26 ||
segments.translation: With the fourth [verse]{pada} he speaks of the [apprehension]{upalambha} of the [true nature]{svarupa}: “Effect…” and the rest. Because he himself is free of [effect and cause]{karya-karana}, the [siddha]{siddha} master [Śāntipāda]{p-santi} speaks of the [unsurpassed]{anuttara} state. For this is reasoning established by [valid cognition]{pramana}: by the [grace]{prasada} of the true [guru]{guru}, the unsurpassed state is known by oneself. So too in the [Hevajra]{tx-hevajra}: “It is known by oneself, through merit, by attending on the succession of gurus.”
segments.note: Munidatta (cp.26.m5) reads the last couplet as the apprehension of the [true nature]{svarupa}: being himself free of [effect and cause]{karya-karana}, Śāntipāda speaks of the unsurpassed state. This, he says, is reasoning established by valid cognition: by the true guru's [grace]{prasada} the unsurpassed state is known by oneself, as the Hevajra says, through merit and attendance on the gurus.

citations.quoted: ātmanā jñāyate puṇyāt guruparvopasevayā: “It is known by oneself, through merit, by attending on the succession of gurus.”
citations.work: Hevajra Tantra, which Munidatta calls the Dvikalpa (cp.26.m5); he quotes this half-verse only, and I have supplied nothing more

flags.note: Bearing on lines 5a and 5b: Munidatta's svayaṃ, ‘himself’, and svayaṃ jñāyate, ‘is known by oneself’ (cp.26.m5), echo the song's sam̐em̐ … bolathi, ‘himself … speaks’, and sam̐beaṇa. He does not use the word svasaṃvedana. Nothing in his paraphrase answers to jaehu jaati in 5a (draft ‘In this world’); the Tibetan line has zung dag, ‘the pair’, there.

guruparvopasevayā: parva(n) means ‘joint, step, section, sacred day’. I follow the Tibetan bla ma'i rim pa nyer bsten pas, ‘by attending on the succession (or stages) of the guru’, with ‘the succession of gurus’; ‘by serving the guru on the sacred days’ is also possible. The Tibetan of the line has gya nom pa nyid bdag gis shes, ‘the excellent itself is known by oneself’. It takes puṇya as ‘the excellent’, the thing known, rather than ‘through merit’, and it reverses the two half-lines.

The edition's daṇḍas separate eṣā hi yuktiḥ from pramāṇopapannā, and svayaṃ kāryakāraṇarahitatvāt from anuttarapadaṃ vadati. pramāṇopapannā is feminine and agrees only with yuktiḥ, so I join them (‘reasoning established by valid cognition’); I also join the second pair as one sentence. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads 'di nyid tshad ma'i rigs pas bskyed pa, ‘this, produced by the reasoning of valid cognition’.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has bla na med pa'i go 'phang du gsungs, ‘spoke as (or in) the unsurpassed state’. For jñāyate it has the honorific mkhyen pa, ‘knows’, which makes Śāntipāda the one who knows. The song number 26 that ends the segment is not translated.

questions: Line 2a (herua): Munidatta's paraphrase (cp.26.m2) has hetvantaraṃ na prāpyate, ‘no further cause is found’, where the refrain has herua ṇa pābiai. The Tibetan line has gzugs, ‘form’. Neither supports ‘Heruka’. Should the song draft carry a reading flag on 2a?

Line 4a (dui māra, bahala): Munidatta (cp.26.m4) has dvayākāra, ‘dual aspect’, and the Tibetan has rnam pa gnyis, ‘two aspects’; neither mentions Māra. The Tibetan also reads bahala as 'bab, ‘flowing’. Should the song draft reconsider or flag ‘two Māras’ and ‘broad’?

Line 3b (caṭāriu): Munidatta (cp.26.m3) glosses it with bādhitam, ‘refuted’. His object is self-grasping as object of meditation and meditator, and what is taken up again is clear light. Is the draft's ‘put a stop to my own self’ close enough, or does it want a note?

Munidatta writes Śānti in cp.26.m1 and cp.26.m5 and Śāntipāda in cp.26.m2 and cp.26.m4. Following the glossary and the song draft, I render all four as Śāntipāda. Should ‘Śānti’ become a listed variant so the commentary can keep his wording?
Munidatta calls the Hevajra the Dvikalpa (cp.26.m3, cp.26.m5). I use the glossary's ‘Hevajra’. Should ‘Dvikalpa’ be added as a variant?

The ‘Chapter on Wisdom’ (cp.26.m2) is unidentified. My guess, flagged as not confident, is the ninth chapter of the Bodhicaryāvatāra; could it be checked? I have supplied nothing beyond the quoted word ‘When examined…’.

Under equations I list only word glosses marked by iti: niravara, śūnye, caṭāriva, and bāla twice. I leave out the passage paraphrases introduced by ‘X ityādi’ (cotton beside body, speech and mind; carding as examination by valid cognition), as the glossary entries tula and dhuni do. Do you want those listed too?

Two doubtful words in the commentary text: sauśīryyante in the Nāgārjuna citation (cp.26.m4), where my ‘hollowness … in the body’ is tentative, and dattvā (cp.26.m3), which may be a slip for dhūtvā. Can the manuscript or another edition be checked?

My transliteration normalises Bengali-script spellings where the word is clear (ḍ for ড়, a single y after r, v or b as the word requires), drops folio numbers, and accepts Shastri's restorations. I leave sauśīryyante as printed.
